title: Farooq Abdullah Demands Killers' Identities Be Revealed After Kashmir Terror Attacks
excerpt: The National Conference president questioned where terrorists are coming from when borders are sealed and urged the UN to assess conditions in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.
body:
• Farooq Abdullah demanded the government reveal the identities of those behind recent terror killings in Kulgam and Anantnag
  • He questioned where terrorists are coming from if all borders are sealed, challenging the claim that terrorism has ended in J&K
  • Abdullah also called for a UN Human Rights Commission delegation to assess conditions in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir
  • J&K Deputy CM Surinder Choudhary demanded a high-level probe and questioned the Centre's post-Article 370 security narrative

National Conference president and former Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah on Sunday demanded that the government make public the identities of the killers behind recent terror attacks in the Kashmir Valley, including the shooting of two migrant labourers in Kulgam and a policeman in Anantnag.

"They (administration) should tell people who is carrying out these killings. All we are told is that terrorists killed them. The question is where the terrorists are coming from when all the borders are sealed," Abdullah told reporters in Bijbehara area of Anantnag district, according to Jammu Bulletin.

"Let us and the whole world see who these killers are. Has terrorism ended? You can see how much the situation has changed."

— Farooq Abdullah, National Conference President

Twin Attacks Spark Political Firestorm

The remarks follow a string of violent incidents that have shaken the Kashmir Valley. On July 31, two migrant labourers from Chhattisgarh were killed in a terror attack in Kulgam district. Ten days earlier, on July 22, Head Constable Ashiq Hussain from Budgam was gunned down in a shoot-and-scoot attack near Lal Chowk on the Anantnag-Kokernag road. Hussain was deployed on security duty for the ongoing Amarnath Yatra. The Resistance Front, a proxy outfit of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba, claimed responsibility for that attack.

Chief Minister Omar Abdullah announced Rs 10 lakh in ex-gratia relief for the families of each of the two Kulgam victims. Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha held a high-level security review meeting on August 1 and directed all Deputy Commissioners and Senior Superintendents of Police to review standard operating procedures.

Deputy CM Questions Centre's Security Claims

J&K Deputy Chief Minister Surinder Choudhary also went on the offensive, directly challenging the Centre's narrative that abrogating Article 370 in 2019 would bring an end to militancy.

"Jammu and Kashmir has been battling militancy for the last 37 years. The Centre revoked the region's statehood, separated Ladakh, and abrogated Article 370 on the promise that terrorism would be eradicated. Six years later, if innocent people are still being killed, the Centre must explain whether its experiment has failed," Choudhary told reporters, according to Jammu Bulletin.

Choudhary alleged a suspicious pattern: both attacks came after the National Conference staged a protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on July 20 demanding statehood restoration. "It appears that someone, whether in Pakistan or elsewhere, is unhappy with the demand," he said, urging Prime Minister Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah to constitute a high-level committee for an impartial investigation.

Spotlight on Pakistan-Occupied Kashmir

Abdullah also turned his attention across the Line of Control. Regional elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir have been marred by violence, with several lives lost. The Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a banned collective of activist groups, has staged demonstrations for nearly two months over 12 contentious seats in the so-called legislative assembly.

"They (PoJK people) are our brothers, and we are pained by what they are going through. The United Nations has a Human Rights Commission. They should send a delegation there to assess the situation first hand," Abdullah said. He expressed surprise at the global silence and noted that even India's own government "has not said anything about it."

What It Means for the Diaspora

The killings of migrant labourers — workers from states like Chhattisgarh who travel to Kashmir for construction and agricultural work — underscore the ongoing vulnerability of internal migrants in conflict zones. For Indians abroad, the attacks serve as a grim reminder that the security situation in Kashmir remains volatile despite years of government assurances. The debate over statehood restoration and counter-terrorism strategy is likely to intensify as Independence Day approaches.

What's Next

Security forces remain on high alert given the ongoing Amarnath Yatra and the approaching Independence Day celebrations. The LG's office has directed a comprehensive review of SOPs across all districts. Whether Delhi concedes to the National Conference's demand for a high-level probe — and whether Farooq Abdullah's challenge to reveal the attackers' identities gains broader political traction — will shape the security and political discourse in J&K in the weeks ahead.
nri_angle: The killings of migrant labourers from Chhattisgarh highlight the vulnerability of internal migrants in Kashmir's conflict zones, reminding Indians abroad that security challenges persist despite government assurances.
